title: Section 1: Euclids Algorithm
text:
Within this weeks lesson, we are going to learn an important algorithm which can be used in more advanced cryptography work, however I am going to try and keep it simple. Then we will look at how to find the modular inverse of a number, which can be used to break an affine cipher. Lastly, we will look at a method which can be used to break any monoalphabetic substitution cipher (which include shift ciphers and affine ciphers).

Section 1: Euclids Algorithm

Who is Euclid?
We will start with a little bit of history about Euclid. Euclid was an ancient Greek Mathematician, who is known as the ‘father of geometry’ due to his study of shapes. He was the first Mathematician who wrote things called ‘axioms’, which you can think of as rules that Maths has to follow. This means he was very important to the development of Mathematics. I would recommend having a little read about him (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid).











What is an algorithm?
‘Algorithm’=‘алгоритм’ An algorithm is a set of instructions which are used to solve a specific problem. They are quite common in Computer Science and Mathematics. You can think of it as like a cooking recipe, if you follow all the instructions correctly and have all the right ingredients, then you will get some wonderful food.


What is Euclids Algorithm?
Euclids algorithm is used to find the greatest common divisor between two numbers. So far we have only used small numbers. For example, we can easily see that the greatest common divisor between 27 and 33 is 3. However, as we use larger numbers, it is going to be harder to find their prime factors meaning it’s harder to find their greatest common divisors. Just as a reminder, if the greatest common divisor of two numbers \(x\) and \(y\) is \(z\), then I would write \(gcd(x,y)=z\). For example, \(gcd(27,33)=3\).
If I asked you to find the greatest common divisor of 10302 and 21726, you might find the answer but it would take a lot of time. Euclids algorithm gives you a quick method. However, before looking at \(gcd(10302,21726)\), we are going to use an easier example to get you familiar with the algorithm.
Before we start the examples, I would like to credit this youtube video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jwf6ncRmhPg). This is the video explains Euclids algorithm very well, and it’s what gave me the idea to represent Euclids algorithm in the way that you’re about to see in the examples. So give it a watch after doing the examples.


Example 1
For this example, each slide represents one of the steps below, so click through the slides and read what they mean at each step.
Find \(gcd(78,102)\) using Euclids Algorithm.
Steps:

First, I want you to imagine that we have got each number in its own area, like what is being shown in the diagram. We can see that there is 78 dots on the left, and 102 dots on the right.
We then look at whichever area has the most amount of dots in, and take away the number of dots from the other side as many times as we can. For this example, we can only take 78 away from 102 once, because if we did it twice then we would have a negative number.
You then write out the new number of dots that you have in each side. We now have 78 does on the left side, and 24 dots on the right side (as \(102-78=24\)).
We then repeat step 2. We can see that now 78 is the side with the most dots, so we take away 24 from 78 for as many times as we can. We take three lots of 24 away from 78, because if we took 4 lots away, then we would have a negative number.
We now have 6 dots on the left side, and 24 dots on the right side.
We can now do our last step, and take away 4 lots of 6 from the right side, to leave us with zero.
We are left with 6 and 0, meaning that the greatest common divisor of 78 and 102 is 6. Our answer is \(gcd(78,102)=6\).


  
  
    ◀ Back
    Step 1 of 7
    Next ▶
  





Now that you have seen an example, it’s time for me to explain some things. - The number on the left and the number on the right will always have the same greatest common divisor. - One of the ways the algorithm ends is by getting a zero in one of the areas. This means that the \(gcd\) is equal to whatever number is in the other box. - The other way the algorithm ends is by getting a one in one of the areas. This means that the \(gcd\) of the two numbers is equal to one (hence the numbers are coprime).
We will now look at an example where the two numbers are coprime, so you can see what happens.


Example 2
Similar to the last example, please click through the slideshow and read through the steps so you know what is happening on each slide.
Find \(gcd(82,65)\) using Euclids Algorithm.
Steps:

Write our two numbers in their two seperate areas.
Notice that 82 is the larger number, so we take away 65 from 82 as many times as we can before we get a negative number. We only take 65 away once, because if we took it away twice then we would get a negative number.
Our new numbers are 17 and 65.
We can see that 65 is now the larger number so we take away 17 from 65. This time, we can only take 17 away from 65 3 times before getting a negative number.
Now we are left with 17 and 14.
17 is our larger number, so we take 14 away from it.
We are left with 3 and 14.
14 is our larger number, so we take 3 away from it.
We are left with 3 and 2.
3 is our larger number so we take 2 away from it.
We are left with 1 and 2. I said earlier that the algorithm ends when we get either a 1 or a zero, and now that we have a 1, we end our algorithm.


  
  
    ◀ Back
    Step 1 of 11
    Next ▶
  



For this example, we can see that we get 1 as one of our final numbers. This means that \(gcd(82,65)=1\), so 82 and 65 are coprime.
When you see these examples, you might think to yourself that I am doing a lot of work for these questions, and you would be right. I am showing you every step that is needed to get the correct answer. However, once you have some practice with these questions then you will be able to do them a lot quicker. In example 2, at step 5 we had 17 and 14 in our two boxes. If you remember that the greatest common divisor of the two numbers in the boxes will always be the same, then you can realise that \(gcd(82,65)=gcd(17,14)\). You might also notice that 17 is a prime number, and the greatest common divisor between a prime number and any other number (except the prime itself) is equal to 1. So you would have been able to stop the algorithm after the 5th step as you would already know that the two numbers had a greatest common divisor of one.
Anyway, it’s time for one last example, but this time we are going to use some big numbers to show you how useful this algorithm is.


Example 3
Find \(gcd(10302,21726)\) using Euclids Algorithm.
As you can see these numbers are quite large, and I do not have the time to create a diagram with twenty thousand dots in, so we are going to do this without a diagram. The algorithm will stay exactly the same, only you will not have the visual help. If you are struggling to understand what is happening without the diagrams, then I recommend having a go at some of the easier practice questions first, then come back to this example.
The first thing we are going to do is take away the smaller number from the larger number as many times as possible. We can see that \(21726\) is larger than \(10302\), so we will do: \[21726-2 \times 10302 = 1122\]
Our new numbers are now, \(10302\) and \(1122\). This means that we do: \[10302- 9 \times 1122=204\]
Our new numbers are now, \(204\) and \(1122\). We now carry on the process and take the smaller number away from the larger one: \[1122- 5 \times 204 = 102\]
Now we have our two numbers as \(204\) and \(102\). Lastly, we can see that: \[204 - 2 \times 102 = 0\] Meaning that the algorithm ends because we have got a zero.
Our final answer is that \(gcd(10302,21726)=102\). I hope you can appreciate that without Euclids algorithm, it would have been very difficult to spot that \(102\) is a factor of both \(10302\) and \(21726\), which shows you how useful this algorithm is.
Some of you may have realised that at the begining I said an algorithm was a set of instructions to solve a problem, however I never explicitly gave you the instructions for this algorithm. I did this because I did not want to confuse you, as it does look a bit difficult if you have never seen it before. Hopefully now you are familiar with some examples, you will be able to understand the instructions easier. The instructions are as follows:

Start with two numbers \(x\) and \(y\) where $x y > 0 $.
Divide \(x\) by \(y\) to get two numbers \(q\) and \(r\) such that: \[x = y \times q + r\] Where \(0 \leq r < y\).
Check the remainder:

if \(r=0\), then \(y\) is the greatest common divisor.
if \(r\) is not equal to zero, replace \(x\) with \(y\) and \(y\) with \(r\), then go back to step 2.


Also, according to these instructions, you only end the algorithm if you have zero as one of you numbers, however I said that you end the algorithm if you have either a zero or a one. Both of these methods will work, because if you see a \(1\) as one of your numbers, then you know on the next step you will have a zero anyways (because every number, \(n\), can be wrote as \(n = n \times 1\)), so my method saves a little bit of time.
Hopefully, you’re familiar with this algorithm now, as it is time for some practice questions!



Practice questions: Euclids algorithm

Use a diagram to find \(gcd(12,26)\) using Euclids algorithm.
Find \(gcd(90,135)\) using Euclids algorithm.
Find \(gcd(60515,26460)\) using Euclids algorithm.
The Dictionary of Chinese Varient Form complied by the Taiwan Ministry of Eduction in 2004 contains 106,230 indicidual characters. I want to create an affine cipher using this alphabet. I have chosen \(\alpha = 85547\). Will this give me a valid affine cipher? Explain why.



Section 2: How to break an affine cipher
In this section we will be looking at some rather difficult Maths, as we will be adding to our knowledge of Euclids Algorithm by introducing the Extended Euclidian Algorithm. We will also introduce the concept of multiplicative modular inverses (I know it sounds scary, but trust me when I say that it’s not that bad).

What is a multiplicative inverse?
Every number has a multiplicative inverse. If I have a number \(x\), then its multiplicative inverse is the number \(y\) such that: \[x \times y = 1\]
For normal numbers (when we are not using mod), this is very easy to calculate. For example, the multiplicative inverse of \(2\) is \(\frac{1}{2}\). We can check this and see that: \[2 \times \frac{1}{2} = 1\]
The multiplicative inverse of \(60\) is \(\frac{1}{60}\), because: \[60 \times \frac{1}{60} = 1\]
The multiplicative inverse of \(-\frac{1}{5}\) is \(-5\), because: \[-\frac{1}{5} \times -5 = 1\]
I could carry on doing these examples, but I think you probably get the idea. For any number \(x\), the multiplicative inverse is \(\frac{1}{x}\), so you don’t even need to do any Maths, you can simply write the same number underneath \(1\) in a fraction.
For a little bit more information, ‘multiplicative’ means that we are multiplying the numbers together (as you can probably guess), and ‘inverse’ means that they equal one. If you study Maths futher you will find that this links heavily with group theory, however we will not look at that now (maybe I will do a course on it if you are interested).
You can also say that if we have some number \(x\), then its modular inverse is \(x^{-1}\) such that: \[x \times x^{-1} = 1\] This is exactly the same as the other definition, only I have swapped \(y\) with \(x^{-1}\).


What is a multiplicative modular inverse?
Note that for this section I have used \(\text{mod 26}\) for the examples, however they will still work if you use another number.
Similar to the last part, we still need two numbers to multiply together to equal one, however the difference is that now we are using modular arithmetic. If I have a number \(x\), then its multiplicative modular inverse under modulo \(26\) is the number \(y\) such that: \[x \times y = 1 \text{ (mod 26)}\]
It can sometimes be very difficult to find the number \(y\), however we have some tricks we can use.
First, we know that \(\text{mod}\) is hard to deal with, so we need to find a way to get rid of it. We can remember that when we have \(\text{mod 26}\) at the end of an equation, all it means is that we are adding (or subtracking) some multiple of \(26\) from either side of the equation. This means that we do this:\[x \times y = 1 \text{ (mod 26)} \implies x \times y + 26 \times n = 1\] where \(n\) is just an integer.
Please take some time to make sure that you understand the step above. We are quickly going to pause this example because we need to understand the Extended Euclidian Algorithm first. Don’t worry though, as we will come back to this.


What is the Extended Euclidian Algorithm?
The Extended Euclidian Algorithm is an algorithm used to find \(gcd(a,b)\) of two numbers \(a\) and \(b\), then it finds the integers \(x\) and \(y\) such that: \[a \times x + b \times y = gcd(a,b)\]
The first thing to notice is that the first half of this algorithm is exactly the same as the Euclidian Algorithm! The Euclidian Algorithm is used to find the greatest common divisor of two number \(a\) and \(b\), so you already know how to use half of this algorithm. We will now look at this algorithm in an example.


Example 1
Use the Extended Euclidian Algorithm on the numbers \(35\) and \(29\).
The first half of this algorithm is just the Euclidian Algorithm, and we know how that works. Using Euclids algorithm, we get: \[35=29 \times 1 + 6\] \[29= 6 \times 4 + 5\] \[6 = 5 \times 1 + 1 \] \[5 = 1 \times 5 + 0\]
The algorithm has finished with \(0\) and \(1\) being the final numbers. This shows that \(gcd(35,29)=1\), so \(35\) and \(29\) are coprime.
We use Euclids Algorithm to change two large numbers into smaller numbers while keeping the \(gcd\) between the numbers the same. This makes it easier to work out the \(gcd\). With the Extended Euclidian Algorithm, we change smaller numbers into larger numbers, while still requiring the difference between the numbers to be equal to one.
In the slideshow below, I will be getting a lot of equations our of seemingly knowwhere. However, all of the equations I get are simply the ones above but they have been rearranged. This is why we need to do the Euclidian Algorithm first. Rearranging the equations above, we can get:\[35=29 \times 1 + 6 \implies 35 - 29 \times 1 = 6\] \[29= 6 \times 4 + 5 \implies 29 - 6 \times 4 = 5\] \[6 = 5 \times 1 + 1 \implies 6-5 \times 1 =1\]
This next slideshow now goes through the Extended Euclidian Algorithm for this specific example. I have used a lot of slides to break it up into smaller parts making it easier to understand.

  
  
    ◀ Back
    Step 1 of 25
    Next ▶
  



This give us our final equation of: \[35 \times 5 - 29 \times 6 =1 \]
This tells us that: \[35 \times 5 - 29 \times 6 = 1 \implies 29 \times 6 =1 \text{ (mod 35)}\]
Now we are going to look at another example, this time in the context of an affine cipher.

title: Section 1: Shift cipher
text:
Lesson 1



Within this weeks lesson, we will learn basic phrases used in cryptography, modular arithmetic and how a shift cipher works.

Section 1: Shift cipher
There are a few words we need to learn first to understand the examples. Within cryptography, people send secret messages to each other. We call the messages plaintext. Remember that the plaintext is what humans can understand and read. As we only want the reciever of the message to understand what it says, we need to turn this message into ciphertext. This ciphertext does not make any sense so anyone who intercepts the message will not be able to understand it. To turn the plaintext into ciphertext, we need to encrypt the message. This encryption will be our secret key that only two people will now. Then to turn the ciphertext into plaintext, the reciever needs to decrypt the message. If this does not make any sense, then do not worry. The example below will help you understand.

Example 1: Shift cipher of 1 using English
Imagine we have the english alphabet,





The English Alphabet




I want to use the alphabet to code a secret message. Alice wants to send the word “Svitlo” to Bob. Alice and Bob have agreed to use a shift cipher of 1. This means that each letter in the plaintext (Svitlo) will move one letter to the right. This can be seen in the diagram below:





Diagram explaining a shift cipher of value one.




For “Svitlo”, the S will become a T, the V will become a W and so on. Meaning we get: \[\text{``Svitlo'' in plaintext}=\text{``Twjump'' in ciphertext}\]
So Alice will send “Twjump” to Bob. Bob knows that Alice has shifted every letter one place to the right so to decrypt the message Bob needs to shift every letter one to the left. By doing this Bob, will successfully decrypt Alices message “Svitlo”.
Earlier we learnt 4 words: - Plaintext: The message you want to send someone - Ciphertext: A string of letters that do not make sense. - Encrypt: Use a key to turn the plaintext into ciphertext. - Decrypt: Use a key to turn the ciphertext into plaintext.
We can demonstrate the relationship between these 4 words using the diagram below.





Diagram explaining plaintext, ciphertext, encryption and decryption.




Now we will look at another example using the Ukrainian alphabet.


Example 2: Shift cipher of 3 using Ukrainian
We will now do a similar example using the Ukrainian alphabet. Suppose Yuliya wanted to send the message “привіт” to Daria using a shift cipher of 3. We can use the Ukrainian alphabet to help encrypt the message.





Ukrainian alphabet.




We are now using a shift cipher of 3, meaning that for each letter we will shift it 3 places to the right. Now we can draw the same diagram as we did in the last question, where the red arrows tell us where each letter maps to.









Notice that I did not draw in all off the red arrows, lots of arrows will make it look confusing and messy. This is why we can use a slightly better diagram. The diagram below has the normal alphabet on top and where each letter is mapped to on the bottom. In other words, we will have the plaintext on the top, and the ciphertext on the bottom.









This diagram makes it very easy to convert between the plaintext and the ciphertext. Using this diagram we can see that encrypting “привіт”, will give us “туйдкх . Unfortunately, I do not speak ukrainian, but I hope that”туйдкх” is not a word and does not make sense by itself. This means that: \[\text{``привіт" in plaintext}=\text{``туйдкх" in ciphertext}\]”
To decrypt the message, you can simply use the diagram the other way around and it will give you the plaintext back.


Practice questions
Hopefully by now you have a basic understanding of what plaintext, ciphertext, encryption and decryption is. We will now put your knowledge to the test with a few practice questions. Also, for now we will only be using a shift cipher, but in the next lesson we will be looking at a different cipher. If you are interested and want to look at it in advance then it is called an affine cipher (but we will look at it next week anyway).

I want to encrypt the word “Ukraine” using a shift cipher 1. What will my ciphertext be?
I have encrypted a word using a shift cipher of 2. My ciphertext is “Nqpfqp”. What is my plaintext?
Encrypt the word “Математика” using a shift cipher of 4.
Explain why a shift cipher of 26 does not work as a cipher? (Using the English alphabet)



Questions to make you think

I have used a shift cipher of 30 to encrypt a message. Which other shift cipher is this the same as? (Using the English alphabet)
How many possible unique shift ciphers are there?




Section 2: Modular arithmetic
This next section is important for studying cryptography, so if you have never seen this before, I encourage you to take your time to make sure you understand this well.
Modular arithmetic is sometimes called “clock arithmetic” because of how we can use a clock to explain it. Imagine we have a 12 hour clock, where the 12 has been replaced by a zero. It would look something like this:









We can see that this clock tells us that the time is 2 o’clock. If wait 8 hours, then the clock will show 10 o’clock, which can be seen below:









This is easy to understand, as \(2+8=10\). But what happens if we wait another 8 hours?
from IPython.display import Image, display display(Image(filename=‘Clock mod example 3.png’, height=350, width=800))
As you can see, waiting another 8 hours means it will go to 6 o’clock. On this clock we cannot have any number which is 12 or greater. This means when we go past the number 11, we have to take away 12 until we get a number between zero and eleven inclusive. So when we add 8 hours the seconds time what we are doing is: \(10+8=18\), but because we know that \(18\) is 12 or greater, then we have to take away 12. When we take away 12 we get \(18-12=6\), which is why the clock shows 6 o’clock. We will now look at a spinner which only has 4 numbers.









We can see that we now have a spinner with only 4 numbers (or if you want then you can imagine it to be some sort of Alien clock). The spinner is currently showing the number 2. If we moved the hand on the spinner 3 times clockwise, then it would end up on the number 1. This can be shown below:









In this case, the calculation we are doing is \(2+3=5\). However the clock does not show the number \(5\) meaning we need to take away \(4\) until we get a number which does appear on the clock. Hence, we do \(5-4=1\) so the clock shows the number \(1\).
Now we need to translate the clock and spinner into Mathematics. When a clock has 12 numbers, we say that we are doing the calculations\(\mod 12\). Writing out the example with the clock Mathematically would look like this: \[2+8=10 \text{ (mod } 12)\] \[10+8=18 \equiv 6 \text{ (mod } 12)\]
In the second example with the spinner (which has 4 numbers), we would write: \[2+3=5 \equiv 1\text{ (mod }4)\]
Now before some practice questions, we will look at some examples.

Example 1
Calculate \(13 + 21 \text{ (mod 26)}\):
First, we will calculate \(13+21\), which will give \(34\). \(34\) is greater than 26 meaning we need to take away 26 until we get a number between 0 and 25 inclusive. \(34-26=8\), meaning that: \[13+21 \equiv 8 \text{ (mod 26)}\]


Example 2
Calculate \(7 \times 5 \text{ (mod 35)}\):
First, we will calculate \(7 \times 5\) which will give \(35\). An important fact to remember is that \(n \equiv 0 \text{ (mod n)}\). This might be a little confusing, but if you think about the clock we saw earlier, it had \(12\) numbers on but only went up to \(11\) as zero was on the clock instead of the \(12\). This means that: \[ 7 \times 5 \equiv 0 \text{ (mod 35)}\]


Practice questions
I’m hoping that this section has not been too difficult for you, however it is still useful to have a go at some practice questions. 1. Calculate \(9+6 \text{ (mod 11)}\) 2. Calculate \(3+7 \text{ (mod 5)}\) 3. Calculate \(6 \times 8 \text{ (mod 20)}\)


Questions to get you thinking

Calculate \(n^n \text{ (mod n)}\)
Try using addition and subtraction under (mod 2). Do you notice anything interesting when using addition and subtraction with the same numbers? Can you explain why this is happening?




Section 3: Shift cipher using numbers
Within this section we will combine what we have learnt in the previous two sections. This will help you to understand cryptography in a more mathematical way. The first step will be to convert our alphabet into numbers, which can be seen in the diagram below:









As each letter now corresponds to a number, we can introduce a new formula: \[ c = p + s \text{ (mod 26)}\] where \(c\) represents the ciphertext, \(p\) represents the plaintext and \(s\) represents the shift. Using this formula, if we wanted to encrypt the plaintext letter “r” using a shift ciphper of 5, then we would first see what number “r” corresponds to. We can see that “r” is represented by 17, so to get the ciphertext we do \(p + s = 17 + 5 = 22\). We can see that \(22\) represents to letter “w”, so using a shift cipher of 5 “r” will get encrypted to be “w”.
Now we will use these numbers to encrypt the word “Svitlo” with a shift cipher of 3.

Example 1
To encrypt “Svitlo” with a shift cipher of 3, we first need do convert all the letters into numbers. So we get, \[\text{``Svitlo"}= 18,21,8,19,11,14\] Then we use the formula and add 3 to these numbers. So we get, \[c=p+s \rightarrow 18+3,21+3,8+3,19+3,11+3,14+3 = 21,24,11,22,14,17\] Now that we have our ciphertext, we will convert it back into letters to give \[21,24,11,22,14,17 = \text{``Vylwor"}\]
Now that we have looked at that example, you might be thinking Why have we bothered to turn the letters into numbers? We can easily do a shift cipher without numbers!, and you would very correct to think this. For a shift cipher it is rather easy to see how the letters will be encrypted, however in future lessons we will look at more complicated ciphers which are not so easy to understand. I have shown you how to turn the letters into numbers with a simple example (shift cipher), so that when we look at harder ciphers you will be able to understand them quicker.
Another reason why we use formulas in encryption is to easily see how to decrypt a message. If we have just recieved the ciphertext from a message, then we can convert it back to the plaintext by rearranging our formula: \[ c = p + s \text{ (mod 26)} \implies p = c - s \text{ (mod 26)}\]
We will now use this idea in an example.


Example 2
You have recived the ciphertext, “ъсaблвр” which has been created using a shift cipher of 15. What is the plaintext?
Before we start this question, I have to point out the obvious which is that for this example we will be using the Ukrainian alphabet instead of the English alphabet. This means that any calculations we do will have to be in \(\text{(mod 33)}\), because the Ukrainian alphabet has 33 letters in. With that in mind, we can start by converting our ciphertext into numbers. We will do this using the following table:









From this table, we can see that: \[\text{``ъсaблвр''}=30,21,0,1,15,2,20\]
Now that we have our ciphertext as numbers, we can use the formula \(p = c - s \text{ (mod 33)}\) to convert from the ciphertext to the plaintext.
\[30-15,21-15,0-15,1-15,15-15,2-15,20-15 = 15,6,18,19,20,5 \text{ (mod 33)}\] Now we can convert these numbers (which represent our plaintext) back into letters to find out what the message was. \[15,6,18,19,20,5=\text{``Леопард''}\]
Now we will finish this weeks lesson with some practice questions.


Practice questions

Encrypt the message “кит” using a shift cipher of 23
Decrypt the message “Xia”, which has been encrypted using a shift cipher of 20.
I am trying to decrypt the message “Gevvsx”. I do not know what shift cipher has been used, but I know that the plaintext “K”, when encrypted, will become the ciphertext “O”. What is the secret message?



Questions to get you thinking

Imagine you and a friend wanted to send secret messages to each other using a shift cipher, and you could both speak perfect English and perfect Ukrainian. Mathematically, which language should you use to make it harder to decrypt your messages? Explain why.

title: Svitlo Cryptography Course
text: Hello Svitlo student, welcome to my lesson course on cryptography! This page will give you a brief overview of the course content, and an explanations of my teaching methods. This course will be different to other courses within Svitlo School, as a lot of the learning will be done outside of the lessons.

title: Section 1: Prime factor decomposition
text: Within this lesson, we will learn about how to find the prime factors of a number. We will then learn the definition of a coprime number. Lastly, you will be introduced to a new cipher!

title: Section 1: Prime factor decomposition
text:
Extension work
I am including this section to answer a question which I had when I first learnt about this topic. Please note that this section is not needed to understand any of the content further on in this course, it is only here in case any of you are interested in learning a little bit more Maths. The question I want to answer is: ‘Why does \(\alpha\) have to be coprime to the number of letters in the alphabet that we’re using?’ 
The first thing we need to ask ourselves is, ‘Why does a cipher work?’, and one of the reasons why a cipher works is because it maps each letter from the plaintext onto one unique letter in the ciphertext. In other words, no two letters in the plaintext will map to the same letter in the ciphertext. If this did happen then it would be impossible to decrypt the ciphertext, as you would not know which letter from the plaintext was used. For example, imagine a cipher mapped the letter ‘A’ and the letter ‘G’ to the letter ‘K’. If I then gave you the letter ‘K’ and asked you which letter in the plaintext was encrypted to give you ‘K’, you would have no idea because it could be either ‘A’ or ‘G’.
So, we know that two letters in the ciphertext cannot be equal to each other if they have come from different plaintext letters. Now to answer our question of why \(\alpha\) has to be coprime, we are going to use a technique called proof by contradiction. If we want to prove that \(\alpha\) has to be coprime with 26 (for the English alphabet), then we need to prove it is impossible to have a valid cipher when \(\alpha\) is not coprime with 26. I know that this might be confusing if you have never seen proof by contradiction before, so if you haven’t, then I would recommend reading about it or asking me in the lesson. Proof by contradiction is a very powerful tool, so if you plan on doing a lot of Maths in the future, then I recommend learning about it now.
Anyway, back to our proof. Imagine we have some affine cipher with an \(\alpha\) which is not coprime to 26. We can now choose two values from the plaintext \(n\) and \(m\) (remember these represent numbers, and not letters). If these did represent the same letters in the ciphertext, then we would get: \[ \alpha n + \beta \equiv \alpha m + \beta \text{ (mod 26)}\]
Immediately we can take away \(\beta\) from both sides to get: \[ \alpha n \equiv \alpha m \text{ (mod 26)}\]
If we know that \(\alpha\) is coprime with 26, then there will be some value of \(\alpha\) which is a factor of 26. There must also be some value of \(n\) such that \(\alpha n\) is equal to a multiple of 26 (for example, \(\alpha\) = 2 and \(n\) =13). This means that if \(\alpha n\) is equal to a multiple of 26, then we will get: \[\alpha n \equiv \alpha m \text{(mod 26)} \implies 0 \equiv \alpha m \text{ (mod 26)}\]
This equation is true when \(n=m\), which is good because if \(n=m\) then we have the same letter in the plaintext being mapped to the same letter in the ciphertext. However, this equation is also true for \(m=0\), which will break our cipher as it means that two different letters in the plaintext are being mapped to the same letter in the ciphertext. We know that \(n\) is not equal to zero as we said earlier that \(\alpha n\) is a multiple of 26, which cannot be true if \(n\) is zero. Therefore, in order to have a valid affine cipher, \(\alpha\) has to be coprime with 26.
